title: Fort Hood Shooter Nidal Hasan Files Court Motion to Block Firing Squad Execution
snippet: Lawyers for Nidal Hasan, the former Army officer convicted in the 2009 Fort Hood massacre, have launched a federal court bid to stall his scheduled December execution.
content:
Attorneys representing Nidal Hasan, the former Army officer convicted in the deadly 2009 Fort Hood shooting spree, have filed a legal challenge in federal civilian court aimed at stopping his scheduled execution by firing squad.

The legal team—backed by the ACLU of Kansas and federal public defenders—filed a motion for a stay of execution on Tuesday to allow time for a habeas corpus petition. The constitutional process requires the federal government to justify a prisoner's detention and sentence in civilian court. Legal scholars note that the filing could tie up the case in lengthy judicial reviews, likely delaying any action well beyond the end of President Donald Trump's administration.

Controversy Surrounding Firing Squad and Broadcast Proposals

The move comes weeks after President Trump approved Hasan's death warrant for December 3 at Fort Hood, Texas, following the exhaustion of his military appeals. The case sparked intense national outcry when Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth initially suggested broadcasting the execution to the public. The idea drew fierce bipartisan backlash from lawmakers, human rights advocates, and religious leaders, who slammed the proposal as barbaric and akin to public lynchings or propaganda used by totalitarian regimes.

Trump later walked back the broadcast idea in a social media post, confirming the execution would proceed by firing squad but would not be streamed. Civil rights attorneys argue that high-ranking officials have improperly turned the legal process into a political spectacle.

A Rare Chapter in Modern Military Justice

Hasan, 56, was paralyzed during his arrest in the 2009 attack that claimed 13 lives and left dozens injured. Defense experts and critics have previously warned that a public execution could play into Hasan's stated desire for martyrdom.

Military executions in the United States are extremely rare. The U.S. military has not carried out an execution since 1961, and it has not used a firing squad since 1945. Hasan is currently one of four prisoners on military death row at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas, awaiting the civilian court's ruling on his stay request.
